title: In Defense of the Bad Guy.
card_title: In Defense of the Bad Guy.
summary: An argument for distinguishing corporate misconduct from the incentives behind innovation.
cover_alt: In Defense of the Bad Guy. — The Private Ledger
body:
Recently, I’ve been seeing a lot of dissatisfaction, disdain and even hatred towards large corporations and the U.S. system as a whole. The fundamentals of U.S. capitalism and the free market as a whole are increasingly being questioned.

And what is being questioned?

America and Western culture and values themselves. Values such as freedom of speech and religion are no longer taken for granted. The ability to start a business and make money has today been deemed evil with anyone wealthy likely seen as someone who is taking advantage of others.

Today, the majority of Americans under 30 say that “most” rich people in the U.S. got rich “by taking advantage of other people.” Seniors (65+) on the other hand, overwhelmingly (72%) believe that wealthy Americans “earned their wealth” without exploiting people.1

And the reason why people are questioning the fundamentals of capitalism isn’t hard to understand. A feeling of rising prices and declining affordability often makes it harder for the average American to see a future where they can buy a house in the city that they grew up in.

Add to this the fact that many companies are reporting record profits and it begins to feel entirely unfair. Nvidia last quarter reported almost $60 billion in net income and Google reported over $110 billion — and that number is growing rapidly every quarter. They aren’t the only ones, Amazon, Meta and Apple all reported record profits in the past year.

Unfortunately, the rise of AI only compounds this feeling of helplessness experienced by many young people who are increasingly worrying about their futures and their ability to make money. The result? An increasing turn towards socialism and disillusionment with capitalism.2 For the first time ever, young Americans have a more favorable view of socialism than capitalism.3

Today, capitalism is becoming increasingly demonized and wealth has become synonymous with evil. Large corporations are seen as entities that first and foremost prioritize profits by taking advantage of society.

In this piece, I want to defend what is now seen by many of my generation as an evil system built to take advantage of the needy.4 I will defend Capitalism itself.

In the beginning of 2026, I was privileged to take a few months off and travel in South-East Asia. I got to experience religions and cultures that I had never had exposure to and view some of the most beautiful nature scenes that exist in the world.

More than anything, the biggest takeaway I had after traveling was that as someone who grew up in the West there was a lot to be thankful for.

I often saw kids as young as eight or nine that weren’t at school and instead were busy spending their days and nights working in family jobs. A particular moment stands out to me while traveling in Luang Prabang, Laos, where I vividly remember seeing a child of around eight or nine on the side of the road washing dishes at his mother’s food stand around noon on a weekday. In Vietnam, almost every restaurant I ate at was run by a family - which often included children working in their early teens.

I came out with a huge feeling of gratitude. I grew up in Toronto where it was unheard of for someone to spend their youth working in order to support a family business rather than being at school. The countries I visited were a different story.

Laos has been communist since its civil war in 1975. Vietnam has been unified as a communist country since 1975 when the North won the Vietnam War which plagued the country for over 20 years.

Today, both Laos and Vietnam have suffered the consequences of decades of anti-free-market socialism. The GDP per capita figures of Laos and Vietnam are respectively $2,400 and $5,120.5

Nearby Singapore, which I was also privileged to visit, on the other hand, has a very different economic system. Singapore has had a capitalist pro-market economy since 1965 and has flourished ever since. Today, its GDP per capita of $107,760 is the seventh highest in the world and the highest of any country not in the Western Hemisphere. It ranks second in purchasing power per capita and despite being only 0.07% of the total world population makes up 3% of my subscribers.

As Margaret Thatcher said in 1976, “The problem with socialism is that you eventually run out of other people’s money.”

Before we analyze examples of Socialism, it is important to define what socialism is. Socialism is defined as “any of various egalitarian economic and political theories or movements advocating collective or governmental ownership and administration of the means of production and distribution of goods.”6

Let’s break that down. Socialism is a spectrum, but the core belief is that a collective, in practice the government, owns the resources of a country and decides how and when to administer and distribute them.

It’s fundamental to understand that. The core principle of Socialism is not advocating for higher taxes for wealthy individuals or healthcare for all. The core principle of Socialism is handing the means of production over to the government.

The result?

Almost always a mix of corruption and incompetence that leads to disaster.

The most famous and largest example of Socialism in practice was the Soviet Union.

And while there were some parts of the Soviet Union that were successful — most notably the ability to mobilize and defeat the Nazi invasion of Russia in WWII — the overall impact was citizens that lived in relative poverty and a mismanagement of food that led to a famine that resulted in the deaths of millions of people.

In the People’s Republic of China, under the rule of Mao ZeDong, the “Great Leap Forward” resulted in the deaths of between 15-50 million people from famine in three years.

In Cuba, a state that has been governed under Socialism since the 1950s, the GDP per capita is $7,381. In the past decade its GDP per capita has actually gone down even before accounting for inflation. In Cuba’s case, the GDP per capita in the 30 years following the implementation of the socialist government increased by roughly 30%. U.S. inflation alone over that same time period grew by 350%.

In Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge, the government went a step further and abolished private property, currency and all markets. The result was a brutal dictatorship that resulted in one of the worst genocides ever. Almost two million people or roughly a quarter of Cambodia’s population were killed or starved due to starvation and overwork.7

Unfortunately, the list goes on. During the twentieth century, hundreds of millions of people suffered under socialist governments.

Boris Yeltsin was a high-ranking member of the Soviet Union’s government who in 1989 took a trip to the U.S. While in Houston, he visited the supermarket Randals. He was blown away by the number of options at the supermarket and later wrote in a memoir that the supermarket visit was one of the key moments that shattered his belief in the Soviet economic system.

In order to understand more about living under a socialist system, I asked my mother who grew up in socialist-run Poland to give her thoughts. Below is part of her response which offers a perspective that I think is critical to understand when looking at socialism from the outside.

“A socialist economy is an economy of constant shortage. There is not enough of mostly everything, and the government is in a constant triage scenario. So who you know may matter more than how much money you have. Because the emphasis is on equity, it also disincentivizes entrepreneurship and hard work. Why sweat if you get paid the same as someone who slacks off? In Poland, we had this saying: ‘They pretend to pay us and we pretend to work.’ The socialist countries of Eastern Europe didn’t exist in a vacuum. Only a few hours away were Germany, France, Austria and Sweden. In the end, people vote with their feet and go where they feel it’s worth working hard and building a better life.

The constant shortages also bred corruption. In Poland, doctors were not paid well, so grateful patients and their families ‘rewarded’ them with the one product that was never in short supply: bottles of alcohol. Mechanics took bribes to ‘procure’ spare parts, and underpaid cops took cash instead of issuing tickets. The whole system worked thanks to the lubricating power of corruption in an economy of permanent shortage. A system in which your hard work is not rewarded, your salary depends on a bureaucrat’s whim rather than the market value of your work, and access to something as basic as an apartment can depend on party membership rather than savings inevitably distorts the value of goods, services and work itself.

The surrealism of everyday life produced two odd side effects: total cynicism and an exceptionally absurd sense of humor. Apartments were in chronic shortage, and it was common for multiple generations of a family to live together in small flats while younger people waited years for a place of their own. I remember a classmate demonstrating pretty impressive actuarial skills calculating how long his grandmother, in whose apartment he lived, was likely to survive. Don’t get me wrong, he loved his grandma, but he was also longing for what we called a ‘de-calcified flat.’ Capitalism rewards entrepreneurs, people who take risks, work hard and come up with new ideas. Socialism has aspirations to create a fairer society. In my experience, it creates a poorer and more backward society. So yes, we were all equally poor. The challenge was not to get equally corrupt.”

However, I believe there is an important note here. I believe many people who want “socialism” don’t actually want true socialism; rather, they want a capitalist society with a better welfare system to protect the vulnerable.

Let me emphasize that point. Many people who believe and preach socialism are younger people who haven’t lived through or seen real socialism in action and therefore their perception of socialism is entirely different from reality.

So let’s shift the conversation.

Does a freer, more market driven economy outperform a more regulated social market economy?

Lucky for us, we have two live examples: The United States and Europe.

And the results are clear.

A 65-page paper called the “The Future of European Competitiveness” found:

“Europe has the foundations in place to be a highly competitive economy…on a per capita basis, real disposable income has grown almost twice as much in the US as in the EU since 2000.”

Furthermore, in the chart below, it is also easy to see how China has bridged and even surpassed the EU since the turn of the century following its adoption of market-oriented reforms and its entry into the WTO.

And it’s not just in income and purchasing power that the EU falls behind, a 2024 study found that EU workers were only 78.5% as productive as their U.S. counterparts.8

In simple terms, U.S. workers are more productive than their European counterparts.

The same paper found that only 0.06% of Europe’s GDP is invested into venture capital. In comparison, the U.S. level was ten times higher.9

The result is that the U.S. has taken a massive lead in innovation and company creation. The chart below shows how many unicorns have come out of each country in the world. Note the incredible disparity between the U.S. and the rest of the world. The U.S. with a population of roughly 350 million people, has started more unicorns than the rest of the world combined 698 vs. 565.

And this disparity only strengthens itself at the top of the food chain. Nine out of the ten most valuable technology companies in the world are based in the U.S and 56 out of the top 100 are based in the U.S. Just a reminder, the U.S. is only 4.2% of the world’s population.

Patrick Collison, the Irish founder of Stripe ,who founded the company in the U.S., recently posted a post on X that perfectly articulated the problem with government overreach.

His closing sentence is a perfect example of why a free market will outperform in the long term. “His second company, needless to say, was not incorporated in Germany.”

So let’s look again at the alternative:

Capitalism and a Free Market.

These systems offer immense opportunity for an individual to become incredibly wealthy and corporations to become incredibly profitable. Additionally, they create a more prosperous society as everyone is directly incentivized to serve the needs and wants of others in order to achieve their own financial gain.

Uber has been the most recent “evil aggressor” being blamed for dynamic and surge pricing. U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren has been a vocal opponent of dynamic pricing, calling it “a way for giant companies to squeeze you even more.”

People criticizing Uber often focus on Uber’s “predatory practices” without realizing a few things.

  1. Uber has significantly increased the quality of life for hundreds of millions of people. Uber often broke the monopoly that taxi systems had, making transportation more convenient and cheaper in the short term by subsidising rides.

  2. In order to do this, Uber had to run a company that was unprofitable for over a decade - this caused more people to use the app over time and Uber to create a moat around convenience and driver availability.

  3. In order to create a large company, the founders and investors had to take enormous risks that their bet would pay off, something they wouldn’t have been incentivized to do in a socialist society.

  4. This risk ended up paying off, both for the founders, investors, and the general public who now benefit from a service that makes their lives more convenient.

  5. This operating system later formed the playbook for other ridesharing companies like Grab, which operates primarily mostly in South-East Asia and recorded its first profitable year in 2025.

For those who dismiss Uber and say that it was all a plot to gain a monopoly, it wasn’t a given that this risk would pay off. Uber reported a negative net income of $8.5 billion in 2019, $6.8 billion in 2020 and $9.1 billion in 2022.

That’s a lot of money lost and it was never obvious that the company would become profitable. In fact, in 2019, Forbes published an article in which they said that “Until and unless Uber can find ways to overcome the numerous weaknesses in its business model, the company will never be profitable.”

That doesn’t sound like the analysis of a monopoly forming. And yet, today, Uber has suddenly become public enemy #1. But there are a number of fundamental questions that have to be asked about Uber and corporations in general:

Is it inherently a bad thing for corporations and shareholders to become incredibly profitable?

What economic function do profits serve and what would happen to investment and innovation if the potential rewards for successful businesses were dramatically reduced?”

I believe that a free market and incentives for companies to pursue record profits actually benefit the average citizen, both directly and indirectly.

Jeff Bezos gets a lot of hatred directed towards him. He’s worth over $250 billion and often gets criticised for using tax loopholes in order to not pay his fair share of taxes. But for a moment, let’s put aside Bezos’s personal tax discussion and take a look at what he has created.

Amazon is a behemoth of a company. In the U.S., it is the second-largest employer employing more than 1.5 million people. The stock has also created tremendous wealth with returns of 282,977% since the stock went public almost three decades ago. More recently, in the past decade, the stock has increased roughly 6x.

Amazon has also significantly improved the quality of life for hundreds of millions of people. The ability to get products delivered to your door within 24 hours is revolutionary. Someone who previously had to spend thirty minutes to pick up an item can now dedicate that time to family time, work or anything else.

More than that, Amazon is one of the largest cloud providers in the world. Netflix, Airbnb, Target and Goldman Sachs all use Amazon Web Services in order to run their businesses.

And so while the exact amount that Jeff Bezos is paying in taxes is certainly debatable, the larger picture is that it is hugely beneficial for Jeff Bezos to have started Amazon and become incredibly wealthy off of it.

I don’t want to pretend that capitalism is perfect. Capitalism with no guardrails can lead to exploitation of workers, lack of care for the environment and a wealth concentration that borders on insanity. Elon Musk is wealthier than almost half of the global population combined.10 That’s almost incomprehensible.

But if Musk’s wealth was capped at $1 billion in 2012, would he have continued to push Tesla and SpaceX forward? Would he have created tens of thousands of jobs? Would he have made tremendous progress both mainstreaming electric vehicles and making great strides towards space technology?

Likely not. And that’s the tradeoff that you make when you adopt capitalism. It is worth allowing Elon Musk to become stupendously wealthy because of the value he creates for society. It is worth having hedge funds and venture capital firms because they invest in technology that makes the world a better place.

“Suppress the reward and you may get a fairer economy, but one that flies at a much lower cruising altitude and at a slower pace. Low and slow is ultimately the most expensive thing a country can be.”

No system is perfect and capitalism is no exception. It can produce inequality and outcomes that feel deeply unfair but it simultaneously drives people to take risk, to innovate and to build.

I, for one, am incredibly grateful that I grew up under a relatively capitalist free-market system that valued and rewarded innovation and hard work.

But before we decide that profit, wealth and inequality are proof that capitalism is broken, we should ask what we would lose by removing the incentives that created so much of the prosperity and innovation around us.

Capitalism has its bad guys. That does not make capitalism the bad guy.

brief.thesis: This essay defends the role of profit incentives and risk-taking in a market economy without claiming that every corporate outcome is fair. It asks readers to distinguish criticism of particular companies from rejection of the broader system that encourages investment and innovation.
takeaways: Successful businesses can follow years of losses and substantial uncertainty.
The author views the rewards for building useful products as an important part of the incentive to attempt difficult things.
brief.risk: The benefits of innovation do not remove questions about inequality, market power, or individual corporate behaviour.
brief.watch: How the essay’s argument applies to the ethical questions raised in the company research elsewhere in this library.

references.text: I refer to the young generation or “Gen Z” as they are called.

As an aside, while in Cambodia I visited the Cambodia genocide museum which was a gut-wrenching experience. Almost a quarter of Cambodia’s population was killed and the prison I attended that housed “traitors and intellectuals” only had 12 to 14 survivors out of 20,000 detainees.
This is from the same source as above - source #9.
